capstone: Design and build a concurrent, tested C++20 utility of your choosing (e.g., a multithreaded file hasher, a parallel word-frequency analyzer, or a small TCP echo server): CMake build with Debug/Release configurations, RAII resource handling with zero raw new/delete, STL algorithms over hand loops, at least one class template or concept-constrained function, a thread pool or worker threads with sanitizer-clean runs (ASan/UBSan/TSan), a CTest suite with meaningful assertions, and a README documenting the C++ standard features used per module and how each sanitizer run came back clean. Deliverable: a git repo link or archive plus a 1-page writeup of the hardest bug the sanitizers caught.
disclaimer: Original study guide keyed to public curriculum; course content itself lives at the source.

checkpoints: Given a linker error message showing 'undefined reference to X', list the three most likely causes and how to check each one.
True or false with justification: a function marked inline in a header can be defined in multiple translation units without violating the ODR.
Explain in two sentences why #pragma once is common practice even though it is not part of the language standard.
keyConcepts: Static vs shared libraries at a high level
Forward declarations and reducing compile dependencies
labs: Take a small C program (hello world plus one helper function in a separate .c file), compile it, then rename the sources to .cpp and compile with g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Werror. Record every new warning and explain each one in your own words.

Deliberately define the same non-inline function in two translation units, link them, and observe the linker error. Then fix it three ways: mark one static, move it to a single .cpp file, and declare it inline.

Introduce a classic missing-symbol bug: declare a function in a header but never define it. Build, read the undefined-reference error, then fix it. Repeat with a variable declared extern but never defined.
Create a tiny C library (add.c/add.h) and call it from C++ using extern "C". Build without the guard first to see mangling break the link (nm to compare symbols), then fix with the guard.
objectives: Explain how a C++ program is compiled: preprocessing, translation units, one-definition rule, and linking.
Read and fix the most common compiler and linker errors (undefined reference, multiple definition, ODR violations).
Set up a sane modern toolchain (g++/clang++) with warnings enabled and a chosen language standard.
modules.title: From C to C++: the compilation model and toolchain refresher

checkpoints: When is the Rule of Zero the right answer, and what two conditions must the member types satisfy for it to work?
Your class manages no raw resources but you define a custom destructor for logging. What happens to the implicitly generated copy operations, and why is that a hazard?
Design question: you need shared ownership with occasional observation that must not extend lifetime. Which smart pointer goes on the observer, and what does lock() tell you?
keyConcepts: Rule of Three (C++98), Rule of Five (C++11), Rule of Zero (C++11 idiom)
Exception safety of destructors (noexcept by default in C++11)
Raw new/delete as a code smell
labs: Write a class FileHandle that opens a FILE* in its constructor and fclose()es in its destructor. Leak a raw handle on purpose (valgrind or -fsanitize=leak if available) to compare, then show the RAII version cleans up even when an exception is thrown mid-scope.

Write a class with a heap-allocated buffer that violates the rule of three (copy it twice, double-free). Observe the crash, then fix it: first with a user-defined copy constructor/assignment, then by deleting copies and adding move operations, then by replacing the raw pointer with std::vector.

Build a parent/child object graph using std::shared_ptr in both directions to create a cycle; print use_count() to show the leak. Fix with std::weak_ptr on the back-reference and verify destruction order with constructor/destructor print statements.
Refactor an existing lab to never call new or delete directly — replace with std::make_unique/std::make_shared — and confirm the program still compiles and passes a smoke run.
objectives: Internalize the rule of three/five/zero and know when each applies.
Implement RAII wrappers that acquire in the constructor and release in the destructor, surviving exceptions.
Use std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, and std::weak_ptr correctly, including the cyclic-reference pitfall.
modules.title: RAII and resource management

checkpoints: You need ordered unique keys with range queries; you need average O(1) lookup with no ordering. Name the container for each and justify.
What does std::remove actually do to a vector, and why must it be paired with erase()?
After v.erase(it) on a std::vector, which iterators remain valid? Contrast with std::list.
keyConcepts: std::vector as the default sequence container
Associative vs unordered containers and their complexity guarantees
constexpr if applied to container choice is not needed — but if constexpr (C++17) helps generic code
labs: Write a word-frequency counter three ways: std::map, std::unordered_map, and std::vector<std::pair> with linear search. Benchmark all three on a 1 MB text file with std::chrono and write up which wins and why.

Take a loop that filters and transforms a vector<int> and rewrite it twice: once with std::copy_if + std::transform, once with C++20 std::ranges::views::filter/transform. Confirm identical output on edge cases (empty input, all-filtered-out).

Write a program that stores iterators into a vector, then push_back enough elements to trigger reallocation, and demonstrate the dangling iterator with ASan (-fsanitize=address). Fix by reserving capacity up front or switching the pattern.

Implement a case-insensitive word search using std::string_view (no copies) over a large buffer, and compare against a std::string version for allocation count using a custom counting allocator or simple instrumentation.
objectives: Choose the right container for the job from vector, deque, list, set/map, and unordered set/map, with complexity reasoning.
Compose generic code with iterators and the <algorithm> library instead of hand-written loops.
Avoid iterator invalidation bugs by knowing which operations invalidate which iterators per container.
modules.title: STL containers, algorithms, and iterators

checkpoints: Explain why std::move does not move anything by itself, and what actually performs the move.
A move constructor that is not noexcept: what penalty does std::vector pay during growth, and why?
Given template<typename T> void f(T&& x), what is the deduced type of T when called with an int lvalue? With an int rvalue?
keyConcepts: Value categories: lvalue, xvalue, prvalue (C++11 taxonomy)
std::move as a cast, not a move
noexcept move operations and their effect on vector reallocation
labs: Write a String class with deep-copy semantics. Add instrumented copy and move constructors that print when called. Run a program that pushes temporaries into a vector and count copies vs moves; then mark the move constructor noexcept and watch reallocations switch from copies to moves.

Write a function template that takes a universal reference and forwards it to two overloads (one taking const T&, one taking T&&). Pass lvalues, rvalues, and const lvalues and print which overload fires each time; fix any case that forwards incorrectly.

Deliberately use an object after std::move and demonstrate that it is in a valid-but-unspecified state (e.g., moved-from std::string). Then write the safe pattern: move, then reassign or destroy, and document the rule.
Measure: return a large vector by value from a function under -O0 with C++14 vs C++17 flags and compare the copy/move constructor call counts to observe guaranteed copy elision.
objectives: Classify expressions as lvalue, xvalue, or prvalue and know which can bind to which reference type.
Implement correct, noexcept move constructors and move assignment operators.
Apply perfect forwarding with universal references and std::forward without reference-collapse mistakes.
modules.title: Move semantics and value categories

checkpoints: What is the difference between a fold expression over && and a recursive variadic base-case implementation, in terms of code you must write?
Why does a concept-constrained template usually give a better diagnostic than the same template with a static_assert inside the body?
Name one thing you still cannot do with templates that requires runtime polymorphism, and when you would choose a virtual interface instead.
keyConcepts: Template instantiation and code bloat awareness
labs: Write a generic clamp/min/max utility as function templates, then intentionally call it with mismatched types (int and double) and read the deduction error. Fix by constraining with a C++20 concept (std::totally_ordered or your own) and compare the error message quality.
Implement a type-safe printf-like logger with variadic templates and a C++17 fold expression. Test with zero, one, and many arguments of mixed types.

Write a fixed-size Matrix class template parameterized on element type and dimensions as non-type template parameters. Add a static_assert that rejects zero dimensions, and a constexpr determinant for 2x2.

Take a template that currently fails deep inside its body for the wrong type, and rewrite it with a requires clause so misuse fails at the call site with a one-line message. Show before/after compiler output.
objectives: Write function and class templates with correct syntax and sensible constraints.
Use variadic templates and fold expressions (C++17) for genuinely generic utilities.
Apply C++20 concepts to constrain templates and produce readable error messages.
modules.title: Templates and generics

checkpoints: Two threads each do x++ on a plain int one million times and the result is 1,432,887. Explain precisely what went wrong at the hardware level, in two sentences.
When is std::atomic the right tool versus a mutex, and what is the one-sentence test?
Your program hangs intermittently. Name the two most likely concurrency causes and the tool/flag you would use to confirm each.
keyConcepts: Memory ordering at a high level (sequential consistency default)
Thread sanitizer (-fsanitize=thread) as the ground truth
labs: Write a counter incremented by 8 threads 1M times each with no synchronization. Run it 5 times, record the varying wrong totals, then rebuild with -fsanitize=thread and capture the race report. Fix with std::atomic and confirm the exact expected total.

Implement a producer/consumer queue with std::mutex + std::condition_variable. Deliberately introduce a deadlock by acquiring two mutexes in opposite order in two threads; detect the hang, then fix with std::scoped_lock and consistent ordering.
Build a tiny thread pool: N workers, a task queue of std::function<void()>, shutdown flag. Submit 100 tasks, verify all run exactly once, then shut down cleanly with all threads joined (no detach).

Take the atomic counter lab and add a second shared variable updated alongside it without synchronization; show with ThreadSanitizer that making only one atomic is insufficient, then protect both under one mutex.
objectives: Launch and join std::thread workers and pass data safely between threads.
Protect shared state with std::mutex/std::lock_guard and avoid deadlocks with consistent lock ordering or std::scoped_lock (C++17).
Use std::atomic for lock-free counters and flags, and explain the data-race rule in plain language.
modules.title: Concurrency: threads, mutexes, and atomics

checkpoints: Why are out-of-source builds the standard practice, and what breaks if you build in-source?
PUBLIC vs PRIVATE in target_link_libraries: what does each propagate, and to whom?
Your CI builds Debug fine but Release crashes. List three build-configuration differences you would check first.
keyConcepts: Targets, not variables: modern CMake practice
labs: Convert a hand-rolled Makefile (or raw g++ commands) project with a lib/ and app/ split into CMake. Build out-of-source, then delete the build directory and rebuild from scratch to prove reproducibility.
Add a third-party dependency via FetchContent (e.g., a small header-only library), link it to one target with PRIVATE scope, and verify a second target does not see its headers (compile-fail test).
Set up two presets or build dirs: Debug with -fsanitize=address,undefined and Release with -O2. Run the same test binary under both and document any behavioral difference you find.
Break the build on purpose: add a new .cpp file without listing it in CMakeLists, observe the stale build, then fix and note the lesson about globbing vs explicit source lists.
objectives: Write a CMakeLists.txt for a multi-target project: library, executable, and tests.
Manage dependencies with find_package and target-based commands (target_link_libraries, target_include_directories).
Configure Debug vs Release builds and pass the project to a second machine or CI cleanly.
modules.title: Build systems with CMake

checkpoints: Your tests pass but ASan reports a heap-buffer-overflow in code the tests cover. Explain how both can be true.
Name the sanitizer for each: use-after-free, signed integer overflow, data race.
In gdb, what is the difference between break, watch, and catch, and when would you use each?
keyConcepts: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (signed overflow, null deref, misaligned access)
gdb: backtrace, frame, print, break, watch
labs: Take a small string-utility module with 3 planted bugs (off-by-one heap overflow, use-after-free, signed integer overflow). Write unit tests that pass despite the bugs, then run the tests under ASan+UBSan and fix each bug the sanitizers report.

Debug a segfaulting program with gdb: run it, take the backtrace, walk up frames, print the offending pointer, and set a watchpoint on the variable that gets corrupted. Write down the exact command sequence you used.

Write a minimal test suite (any lightweight framework or hand-rolled asserts) for the Matrix class from the templates module, wire it into CMake via CTest, and make the full build fail on test failure.
Plant a data race in test-adjacent code, run the suite under ThreadSanitizer, read the race report (which two threads, which memory location, which stack traces), and fix it.
objectives: Write unit tests for C++ code with a lightweight framework and run them under CTest.
Use AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and ThreadSanitizer to find bugs tests miss.
Drive gdb (or lldb) to get backtraces, inspect variables, and set conditional breakpoints.
modules.title: Testing and debugging: sanitizers, gdb, and unit tests

objectives: Close the gap from C to modern C++: write idiomatic, resource-safe code using RAII, move semantics, and the STL.
Build, test, and debug a multi-file C++ project with CMake, sanitizers, and gdb on a home machine or free-tier CI.
Apply concurrency primitives (threads, mutexes, atomics) correctly and reason about data races and lifetimes.
Design generic, reusable components with templates and know which features come from C++11, 14, 17, and 20.
title: Modern C++ Engineering — Study Sequence
